Headline: More than €4 billion needed for road and rail repairs, says Finland's infrastructure agency
Full_Text: The Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency estimates that some 4.3 billion euros worth of repairs are overdue on Finland's railways, roads and waterways. The estimated cost of the Finnish state's backlog of needed repairs to roads, railways and waterways rose by more than 100 million euros last year. The Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency published its latest data on Monday. The agency said that the price tag for the total backlog of repairs now adds up to almost 4.3 billion euros. That would cover the cost of fixing infrastructure that is in poor or very poor condition. It covers state-owned transport routes, not municipal streets or private roads, for instance. At the end of last year, by far the largest chunk of this ‘repair debt’ was for state roads, which the agency says need over 2.6 billion euros in maintenance. A large proportion of this is for less-used roads. The rail network needs approximately 1.6 billion euros in repairs while 29 million euros should be spent to maintain water transport routes, the agency said. The figure for waterways is virtually unchanged from last year’s report. The Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency has updated its repair needs calculation annually since 2016, with the shortfall in needed expenditures increasing practically every year. Headline: Finland to introduce 'green wave' automated system for emergency vehicles
Full_Text: Fintraffic’s national traffic priority system, which is set to be introduced this summer, will recognise the location of an emergency vehicle and automatically change the lights to green to facilitate its passage. Finland's traffic authority Fintraffic is preparing to roll out a new traffic lights system across the country, which will give priority to emergency vehicles. The automated system will allow ambulances, fire trucks, and other emergency response units to pass through intersections via a 'green wave' of lights. In a press release, Fintraffic explained that the initiative is intended to speed up emergency response times and reduce the risk that emergency vehicles get stuck at busy intersections. The so-called national traffic light priority system, which is set to be introduced this summer, will recognise the location of an emergency vehicle and automatically change the lights to facilitate its passage. "All cities, municipalities, and wellbeing services counties are welcome to join the national traffic light priority system. The aim now is to implement a nationwide green wave for rescue and emergency units, enabling them to get help to the scene safely and quickly," Juho Neuvonen, Fintraffic’s Product Manager, explained in a press release on Monday. Although the new system will be officially in operation from July, rolling it out across the country will take time as traffic systems are tested and updated. The plan follows a successful pilot project. "About 700 intersections and 300 emergency vehicles were involved in the pilot phase. No emergency-related accidents occurred at the intersections included in the pilot. This demonstrates the system’s effectiveness in practice, and its impact is especially evident in congested areas where every moment is crucial for rescue and emergency units," Neuvonen said. Headline: Mind your head — Finns top EU charts for bike helmet usage
Full_Text: Roadside observations found that more than 70 percent of Finnish cyclists used a helmet, compared to just 5 percent in the Netherlands. People in Finland are the most conscientious users of bicycle helmets in Europe, according to the results of a comparative study of 25 EU member states. Finland's data was collected by the VTT Technical Research Centre, with roadside observations revealing that more than 70 percent of Finnish cyclists used a helmet. According to a VTT press release, this put Finland ahead of the 16 other countries in which helmet-wearing habits were researched. By contrast, the corresponding figure in the Netherlands was just five percent. The study also found that, in all countries, the use of bicycle helmets was less common in urban areas than in rural regions. Although Finns scored highly on the wearing of bike helmets, the study found other areas of road safety where there is significant room for improvement. For example, speeding by motorists — especially on rural roads with a speed limit of 80 km/h — was found to be of particular concern. Only 35 percent of Finnish drivers on such roads complied with the limit, according to the results of the study. "Speeding continues to be a significant road safety challenge in Finland, and more efforts should be made to prevent it," VTT Research Team Leader Fanny Malin noted. "This is why the additional recommendations state that effective measures, such as monitoring, communications and infrastructure solutions, should be developed to prevent speeding." As part of the project, road safety in Finland was assessed based on six key performance indicators (KPIs): compliance with speed limits, seat-belt use, cycling helmet use, drink-driving, vehicle safety, and the time elapsed between notification of a road traffic accident and the arrival of the first rescue unit at the scene of the accident. Compliance with speed limits was the only KPI in which Finland scored comparatively poorly. Headline: Over 4 million tune into Finnish radio every week, survey finds
Full_Text: Radio listenership remains steady, reaching over 80 percent of the population each week. Two of the top three stations are Yle outlets. Radio listenership in Finland is alive and well, according to the results of a survey by Finnpanel, a media market research firm. The latest National Radio Survey revealed that more than four million people in Finland listened to the radio every week last year, meaning that the medium reached over 80 percent of the population during an average week. This is similar to the results of the previous year's survey, showing that radio listenership remains steady. In terms of the most popular radio stations last year, Yle Radio Suomi topped the charts by reaching 30 percent of the population on a weekly basis, while commercial station Radio Nova came in second. In third was Yle Radio 1, which carries a mix of music and talk, including the daily News in English. Overall, commercial stations reached some 3.4 million people weekly, while 2.3 million tuned in to Yle's offerings. Breaking down last year's data further, the most popular listening time was 9am, when about one million people usually tuned in. People also tended to listen to an average of about two hours of radio per day, typically dividing that time between one or two stations. People aged over 55 were particularly avid listeners, tuning in for about three and a half hours a day. The most common place people listened to the radio was at home, with in the car being second and at the workplace in third. Podcasts were also increasingly popular, especially among younger people, with nearly one in three 15–24-year-olds listening to podcasts weekly. Yle News broadcasts daily news bulletins on Yle Radio 1 at 3:55pm and on Yle Mondo at 3:30pm. The bulletins are also available to listen to on Yle Areena and on the Yle News home page. Finnpanel conducts the National Radio Survey annually. The listening data is collected year-round from about 18,000 respondents’ habits, covering over 120,000 listening days in total. Headline: Wednesday's papers: Security-minded Finns, Everyone's Rights confusion, and it's not just the weather that's cold
Full_Text: Some people seem to have forgetten the rules regarding Everyone's Rights. People in Finland are more concerned about security issues than their European counterparts, according to results of the latest Eurobarometer survey carried out on behalf of the European Parliament. The Social Democrats' newspaper Demokraatti reported the results, noting that nearly 80 percent of Finns said they were concerned about security, while 70 percent of all EU citizens said they felt the same. Finns were also more likely to want more resources to stave off international threats. Some 90 percent of people in Finland favoured additional resources, while 70 percent of those in other European countries were of the same opinion. In addition to concerns about security and terrorism threats, around two-thirds of EU citizens said they were concerned about climate-change related disasters, cyberattacks and migration, according to Demokraatti. A vast majority (90%) of all respondents said EU states should be more united to meet current global challenges. When asked what issues they would like the European Parliament to raise, curbing inflation and living costs came in first place, with about 40 percent of respondents saying so. Around the world, Finland is famous for a few things: it is the happiest country on earth (at least for the past eight years), it is the spirtual home of the sauna, and it has something called Everyone's Rights. The term (which until a farily recent gender-neutral change) used to be Everyman's Rights — or jokamiehenoikeudet in Finnish — and refers to a tradition allowing people the right and freedom to move around in nature and use natural resources without having to own the land in question. But it seems people in Finland are forgetting the rules surrounding those rights, according to Swedish-language daily Hufvudstadsbladet. Last weekend the paper published an article about a couple who live in the Tammisaari archipelago in Southern Finland. The couple claimed that visitors to the island-dotted area have been behaving worse than in the past. Among other things, the couple told HBL that last summer they filled 20 large garbage sacks full of litter they collected from their group of islands that was left behind by visitors. In addition, visitors have also built campfires on the land, a practice which is not part of Everyone's Rights. To light any type of fire on property that is not your own requires the permission of the landowner, HBL pointed out. The couple told the paper they think people's behaviour has gotten so bad, that they would like to be able to limit the public's access to the islands. As a follow-up, the paper sought out nature conservation and recreation specialist Miliza Malmelin from the Ministry of the Environment. Malmelin has worked in the field for the past decade, but told the paper that she hasn't noticed an increase in troublesome visitors or misunderstandings of the Everyone's Rights rules. She however agreed that lighting campfires or grilling on someone else's land without permission is absolutely unacceptable. Furthermore, overnight visitors on someone else's property should stay a couple of days at the most. While public access rights are not written in lawbooks, that's the general rule. Stays lasting a week are clearly excessive, according to Malmelin. Generally speaking, she said that restricting public access laws would be a major change for Finland, adding that Everyone's Rights offers "people equal opportunities in ways that private ownership never could". The communications chief at Finland's natural resource — and national park management — firm Metsähallitus, Harri Karjalainen, told the paper that he thinks that people aren't as familiar with the rules surrounding public access as they used to be. "Not everyone knows what you can and can't do in nature," he told the paper. According to Metsähallitus, around 3.5 million people visited the country's national parks. Some 51,000 of those visits were made to the Tammisaari Archipelago National Park. Karjalainen noted that people increasingly headed out to the countryside and forests during the Covid pandemic. That was a positive development, he noted, but it also led to many new visitors that may not be familiar with the rules. "We have received some feedback saying that people don't know how to behave now," he told the paper. The firm has received complaints about littering, people letting their dogs run free, as well as about visitors building fires without permission. Metsähallitus used a campaign to remind people about the rules that need to be followed at national parks, but some of the guidelines can be used in other areas too, according to the paper. But the campaign effort has not been active recently, even though its posters and related information can still be seen at the parks. Raising questions about everyday aesthetics, Helsingin Sanomat spoke with lighting designer Håkan Långsted who thinks that lighting should make people feel good rather than bad. However, he also thinks that is rarely seen in Finland's public spaces. The country's health centres, transport and shopping centres are all very brightly lit with lighting that is white, flat and nearly contrast-free. There is usually no accommodation made to create a positive atmosphere, according to Långsted. But the paper asks why. According to Elisa Hillgen, chair of the Illuminating Engineering Society of Finland, it is because "public spaces are used by people of all ages and types, the design starts from the assumption that lighting should be accessible, meaning we think about it from the perspective of the most vulnerable ones". She told the paper that to people with normal vision the bright lights can seem excessive. Lighting in Finland's public spaces is generally based on EU rules, with a few exceptions. However, Hillgen noted, changing the colour temperature of lighting does not in itself reduce visibility. Instead, different light sources and colour temperatures have the potential to make shades and contrasts less distinct. But warmer colour temperatures in themselves are not a major safety risk, according to Hillgen. The reason public spaces are often lit with 4000-degrees Kelvin (very cold white) lighting, stems from a bygone era, when cool-toned lightbulbs produced more light per watt than warm-toned bulbs. Now, in the era of modern LED lighting, the difference in energy consumption levels of bulbs with different colour temperatures has shrunk to such a small degree that using cold lighting cannot be justified on energy conservation grounds, according to the paper. According to Hillgen , technology has made it possible to take other considerations into account when planning lighting for public spaces. Both Hillgen and Långsted think the situation is set to change, with aesthetics possibly taking a larger role in such planning. "Lighting should offer a feeling of it being on your side," Långstedt said.
